title: Consumer lending model at a retail bank
body: Meridian Retail Bank operates in the United States and, through a small subsidiary, in Ireland. Its Credit Products group has built a machine learning model that scores applications for unsecured personal loans. The model does not approve or decline on its own: it returns a score band, and underwriters hold final authority. In practice, underwriters follow the score band in roughly 94% of cases, and the underwriting handbook instructs them to record a written justification only when they depart from it.

The model was developed in-house on eleven years of the bank's own lending history. The data science team removed race, sex, age and postal code from the feature set before training. Remaining features include debt-to-income ratio, length of credit history, employment tenure, number of recent credit enquiries, and the applicant's device type at the point of application.

The bank has an AI governance committee chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, with standing members from Legal, Compliance, Model Risk Management, Data Science and the first-line business. Model Risk Management runs an independent validation before any model goes live, and owns the model inventory. The Credit Products group owns the business outcome and funds the work.

Pre-deployment validation was completed nine months ago and the model went live shortly after. Validation covered discrimination performance, stability, and a fair-lending review that tested outcome rates across protected classes using proxy inference on the applicant population. No disparity exceeded the bank's internal threshold at that time.

Last month's quarterly monitoring pack showed two things. First, the model's discrimination performance has degraded modestly but remains inside tolerance. Second, and separately, approval rates for applicants in one metropolitan area have fallen 14 percentage points relative to the same quarter last year, while approval rates elsewhere are flat. The area in question has a substantially higher share of one racial group than the national average. Model Risk Management has not yet established whether the shift is driven by the model, by a change in the applicant mix, or by an unrelated change to the bank's marketing spend in that region.

The Credit Products group has asked the committee to approve an expansion of the model to small-business lending next quarter, arguing that the underlying creditworthiness signal is the same and that a second validation would duplicate work already done.

facts.value: In production nine months; expansion proposed

facts.label: Human oversight
facts.value: Underwriter override available; followed 94% of the time

facts.value: United States; Ireland (subsidiary)

facts.label: Model ownership
facts.value: Credit Products (business); Model Risk Management (validation, inventory)

facts.label: Monitoring signal
facts.value: Regional approval rate down 14pp; cause not established

facts.value: Removed from features before training

title: Procured résumé-screening tool at a logistics firm
body: Calderon Freight employs 18,000 people across warehouse, driving and corporate roles. Talent Acquisition has licensed a résumé-screening product from an external vendor to handle the first pass on warehouse applications, which run to about 40,000 a year. The tool ranks applicants and surfaces the top 20% to a recruiter. Applicants outside the top 20% are not seen by a human unless a recruiter searches for them specifically.

The vendor built and trained the model. Calderon supplied no training data and cannot inspect the model weights or the feature set. The vendor supplies a model card, a summary of an annual third-party bias audit, and an SLA covering uptime and support response. The contract was negotiated by Procurement with input from Legal; the AI governance function was not consulted before signature, because the tool was classified as a recruitment SaaS purchase under the existing vendor policy.

Calderon configures the tool by uploading a job description and selecting weightings across three sliders labelled 'experience', 'reliability signals' and 'role fit'. What sits behind each slider is not documented beyond a one-paragraph description in the product help centre.
Calderon operates in several US states and has a small distribution site in the Netherlands that uses the same tool for warehouse hiring.

Six weeks into use, a recruiter notices that applicants whose résumés show employment gaps of more than four months are almost never surfaced, including several who went on to be hired successfully through referral. Nobody at Calderon configured a rule about employment gaps. The vendor's bias audit summary reports no adverse impact on race or sex, and does not mention employment history.
Calderon's Chief People Officer wants to expand the tool to driver hiring, where a licence check and a regulated safety record already form part of the process.

facts.value: Calderon deploys; the vendor develops and trains

facts.value: Only the top-ranked 20% reach a recruiter

facts.value: Multiple US states; Netherlands site

facts.value: Model card; annual bias audit covering race and sex only

facts.value: Employment-gap applicants rarely surfaced; not a configured rule

facts.value: Not consulted before contract signature

title: Generative assistant for a municipal benefits agency
body: The Department of Housing Support for a city of 900,000 residents administers rental assistance. Caseworkers field about 3,000 enquiries a week. The department has piloted an assistant built on a commercial large language model, accessed through the provider's API, that answers caseworker questions about programme rules by retrieving from the department's own policy manuals and returning a drafted answer with citations.

The assistant is used by caseworkers, not by residents. A caseworker reads the drafted answer, checks the cited passage, and then communicates with the resident in their own words. Nothing the assistant produces reaches a resident directly, and it plays no part in deciding eligibility.

The department is the deployer. The model provider is a general-purpose AI provider and offers no commitment on model version stability beyond 90 days' deprecation notice. The retrieval index is built and maintained by the department's own IT team from the current policy manuals, and is rebuilt nightly.

During the pilot the department logged every query and every drafted answer. Review of a 400-item sample found that 6% of drafted answers cited a policy passage that did not support the claim made in the answer, and a further 2% cited a passage that had been superseded by a policy change the index had not yet picked up. In every one of those cases the caseworker caught the problem before speaking to a resident, because checking the citation is a required step.

The department's records-retention schedule requires that any record forming part of a benefits determination be retained for six years. Enquiry logs currently roll off after 30 days. Legal has raised, but not resolved, whether a drafted answer that a caseworker relied on becomes part of the determination record.
The city council has asked for a public statement about how AI is used in the department before the assistant moves from pilot to full deployment.

facts.value: Department deploys; a general-purpose AI provider supplies the model

facts.value: Internal caseworkers only; no resident-facing output

facts.value: No part in eligibility determination

title: Remote proctoring at a public university
body: Northbridge University is licensing a remote proctoring tool for online examinations. The tool records the candidate's webcam and screen, and flags 'anomalies' — gaze direction away from the screen, a second face in frame, background noise above a threshold. Flagged sessions are queued for review by an academic integrity officer, who decides whether to open a misconduct case.

The vendor states that the tool 'does not make decisions about students' and that flag rates are comparable across demographic groups. It supplies no breakdown behind that claim. Northbridge asked for one during procurement and was told the analysis is commercially confidential.

The university's disability services team has noted that several conditions produce atypical gaze patterns, and that students with those conditions currently receive exam accommodations arranged case by case with the examinations office.

facts.value: University deploys; vendor develops

facts.label: Human review
facts.value: Every flag reviewed before any case opens

facts.label: Vendor evidence
facts.value: Parity claim asserted; underlying analysis withheld

facts.label: Known interaction
facts.value: Some disabilities produce atypical gaze patterns

title: Dynamic pricing at a cross-border retailer
body: Vantor operates an online marketplace serving customers in Canada, the United Kingdom and Germany. Its pricing team has deployed a model that adjusts listed prices for its own first-party goods several times a day, using inventory levels, competitor prices, historical demand curves and session-level signals including the customer's approximate location and device.

Prices are not personalised to an identified individual — every customer in the same location band and device class sees the same price at the same moment. Vantor's public pricing policy says prices 'vary with demand and availability' and does not mention the model.

Legal has raised that the session-level signals mean two customers in the same city can be shown different prices at the same moment, and that approximate location correlates with income in several of Vantor's markets. The pricing team's position is that the model optimises margin and was never given any protected attribute.
The model is retrained weekly on the previous eight weeks of transactions, including its own prior pricing decisions. No one has assessed whether the retraining loop reinforces its earlier choices.

facts.value: Canada, United Kingdom, Germany

facts.label: Personalisation
facts.value: Segment-level, not individual

facts.label: Disclosure
facts.value: Public policy mentions demand and availability only

facts.label: Retraining
facts.value: Weekly, on data including its own prior decisions

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: Inventory, competitor prices, demand history, location band, device class

title: Predictive maintenance and automated dispatch at a utility
body: Ardal Power operates regional electricity distribution for about 2.1 million customers. It has run a predictive maintenance model for four years that ranks transformers by failure likelihood; field crews use the ranking to plan inspection routes. That system is well understood, validated annually, and has a documented override rate of about 18%.

Ardal is now piloting an extension: an automated dispatch agent that reads the same ranking, checks crew availability and parts inventory, and issues work orders directly to crew tablets without a planner in the loop. The stated goal is to cut the lag between a ranking update and a crew arriving. A planner can cancel a dispatched order, but orders are issued continuously and no planner reviews them before issue.

During the eight-week pilot, the agent issued 4,100 work orders. Planners cancelled 61. Of those, 44 were cancelled because the agent had dispatched a crew to a site where another crew was already working — the agent reads inventory and availability from a system that updates every 15 minutes, and the crew management system updates in real time.

Ardal's regulator requires it to demonstrate that maintenance decisions affecting supply reliability are traceable to an accountable person. Ardal's existing evidence for this is the planner's name on each work order. Under the pilot, work orders carry the agent's identifier.

The engineering lead argues the 61 cancellations out of 4,100 show the agent is performing well. The operations director notes that the 15-minute staleness has a known worst case that has not yet occurred: dispatching a crew to a transformer that another crew has already de-energised for work.

facts.label: Established system
facts.value: Ranking model, four years live, ~18% override rate

facts.label: Pilot
facts.value: Automated dispatch agent, no planner before issue

facts.label: Pilot volume
facts.value: 4,100 orders; 61 cancelled; 44 were duplicate dispatches

facts.label: Data staleness
facts.value: Availability and inventory refresh every 15 minutes

facts.label: Regulatory duty
facts.value: Maintenance decisions traceable to an accountable person

facts.label: Current evidence
facts.value: Planner name on the order; agent identifier under the pilot

title: Model risk in a general insurer's claims operation
body: Kestrel Mutual settles about 240,000 motor claims a year. It has deployed a model that triages incoming claims into three lanes: straight-through settlement for low-value, low-complexity claims; standard handling; and referral to the special investigations unit. Only the third lane has a material adverse consequence for a customer — a referred claim is held while investigated, typically for eleven days.

The model was validated before launch and is monitored monthly on referral rate, straight-through rate and settlement cost. It has run for two years without a validation refresh, on the basis that monitoring has stayed inside tolerance.

A recent internal review found that referral rates for claims from three postcodes are roughly double the book average. Those postcodes were not features. Two of them have among the highest recorded fraud rates in the insurer's own history; the third does not, and has a demographic profile unlike the other two.

Kestrel's fraud team regards the referral model as its most valuable tool and points to a measurable fall in fraudulent payouts since launch. Its customer ombudsman liaison notes that complaints about claim delays have risen over the same period, and that the complaints cluster geographically.

title: Foundation-model assistant inside a software company
body: Halden Systems builds developer tooling. It has embedded a commercial foundation model into its product as an assistant that explains code and proposes fixes. Halden does not train the model; it sends the customer's code as context at inference time and returns the response.

Halden's contract with the model provider permits commercial use and states that inputs are not used for training. Halden's own customer contracts predate the assistant and describe the product as processing customer code solely to provide the service.

A prospective enterprise customer has asked three questions Halden cannot currently answer from documentation: which sub-processors receive their code, where inference happens geographically, and what happens to their code if the model provider changes its terms.
Halden's engineering lead notes the assistant materially improves resolution times. Its head of legal notes the customer contracts were written before any third party saw customer code.

facts.value: Halden deploys and redistributes; the provider supplies the model

facts.value: Customer code sent as inference context, not for training

title: Automated grading pilot at a school district
body: The Brightwater district is piloting automated scoring of written responses on interim assessments across 42 schools. Scores inform instructional grouping for the following term; they do not appear on transcripts and carry no graduation consequence.

The vendor's model was trained on responses from a different state, scored by that state's rubric. Brightwater's rubric differs in how it weights evidence use. The vendor says the models are 'rubric-agnostic'.

During the pilot, teachers may override any score. Override data shows teachers overrode 3% of scores overall, but 11% for responses from students designated as English learners, almost always upward.
The district's assessment director wants to expand to end-of-course exams next year, where scores do affect placement and, indirectly, course access.
